title: Waste is becoming a visible test of consumption growth, municipal capacity, public health, climate resilience and circular-economy opportunity
source_unit: World Bank Group, What a Waste 3.0: Global Snapshot of Solid Waste Management toward Circularity until 2050
geography: Global municipal solid-waste system analysis using publicly accessible data from 217 countries and economies and 262 cities

waste_2022.unit: metric tonnes of municipal solid waste generated globally in 2022

waste_2050_bau.unit: metric tonnes projected under business as usual in 2050

growth.unit: percent increase in global municipal waste between 2022 and 2050 under business as usual

driver.value: population growth, urbanization, rising incomes and increased consumption are driving waste faster than local systems can absorb

observations.method: World Bank global reference dataset and scenario analysis covering waste generation, composition, collection, treatment and disposal.
observations.uncertainty: The 2050 figure is a scenario projection dependent on population, income, consumption, policy and waste-intensity assumptions; country and city data quality and definitions vary.
observations.subgroup: Households, consumers, cities, municipal systems, producers, waste workers and communities exposed to waste pollution, flooding, health risks or service gaps.
observations.counterinterpretation: Waste prevention, source reduction, reuse, repair, recycling and circular production can decouple waste volumes from population and income growth; the business-as-usual path is not inevitable.

denominator.unit: countries and economies in the What a Waste 3.0 reference dataset

low_income_collection.unit: percent of waste collected in low-income countries, as reported in the World Bank global snapshot

high_income_collection.unit: approximately percent collection rate reported for high-income regions

mismanaged_waste.value: approximately one-third of global municipal waste is not properly collected or treated

regional_gap.value: Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia face rapidly growing waste volumes alongside weaker infrastructure and more constrained municipal budgets

observations.method: Comparative World Bank estimates of collection, treatment and disposal across income groups, countries and cities.
observations.uncertainty: Collection and proper-treatment measures are not interchangeable; national averages conceal city, neighborhood and informal-sector variation, and some underlying data are estimated or incomplete.
observations.subgroup: Low-income and rapidly growing urban populations, informal-settlement residents, waste workers, neighborhoods near dumping or burning, and households lacking reliable municipal services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Informal recovery networks can provide important collection and material-recovery functions where formal systems are weak, though workers may face severe health, income and recognition risks.

observations.period: 2022–2050; fiscal, economic and employment dimensions of waste systems

denominator.unit: global municipal waste-management cost and employment synthesis

current_cost.unit: US dollars in annual global municipal waste-management costs, approximately

2050_cost.unit: US dollars in projected annual global municipal waste-management costs by 2050

low_middle_income_investment.unit: US dollars in estimated waste-system investment needed across low- and lower-middle-income countries between 2022 and 2050

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of municipal waste costs, employment, public expenditure, infrastructure needs and circular-economy opportunities.
observations.uncertainty: Cost and investment figures depend on service standards, technology, financing, wage, disposal and scenario assumptions; the worker estimate includes formal and informal activities and is not a measure of decent-work quality.
observations.subgroup: Municipal governments, taxpayers, service providers, formal and informal waste workers, recyclers, manufacturers, households and firms dependent on functioning urban infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher investment can reduce long-run costs and create jobs, but without cost recovery, worker protections, producer responsibility and accountable contracting, spending may not improve service quality or inclusion.

observations.period: 2050 scenarios; circularity, climate and public-system ambition

low_ambition_waste.unit: metric tonnes projected global waste in 2050 under the low-ambition scenario

high_ambition_emissions.unit: metric tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent projected from the waste sector in 2050 under the high-ambition scenario

bau_emissions.unit: metric tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent projected from the waste sector in 2050 under business as usual

intervention_set.value: waste prevention, source reduction, collection, recycling, composting, sanitary landfilling and stronger regulation can bend the waste curve

observations.method: World Bank alternative-scenario modeling of waste generation, service expansion, treatment, disposal and waste-sector emissions.
observations.uncertainty: Scenario outcomes are not forecasts and depend on coordinated policy, finance, infrastructure, behavior, markets and regulatory implementation; emissions accounting and circularity benefits vary by technology and context.
observations.subgroup: Cities, households, producers, waste workers, recyclers, climate and environmental agencies, local communities and investors in circular systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Circularity can be oversold if it substitutes downstream recycling for upstream reduction, shifts pollution to poorer places or leaves informal workers without recognition, safety or bargaining power.

related_sources.claim: World Bank open country and city waste database accompanying What a Waste 3.0.
World Bank summary of report launch, global data frame and policy relevance.
World Bank solid-waste management overview and key findings.

boundary: This record adds a consumption-to-public-infrastructure route: waste volumes, collection, treatment, municipal finance, public health, flooding, jobs, emissions and circularity are analyzed as one system. It is a global technical reference and scenario dataset, not household consumption microdata, a behavior-change evaluation, a city service audit or proof that circular-economy jobs are decent or equitably distributed.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank What a Waste 3.0 page, solid-waste overview, launch brief, open-data catalog and full report PDF were reviewed for global waste generation, collection gaps, costs, employment, investment needs and alternative scenarios; the full report PDF was hashed.
